opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is really the heart of what we looked at in the "Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?" work. When people plot performance against scale and see this flat line near zero for small models, then a sudden jump at some size, the natural reading is that the small models just don't have the capability at all, and then something qualitatively new switches on. Our interpretation is that, in many cases, that flat region is more a property of the measurement than of the model.

The key issue is the choice of metric. A lot of the tasks where emergence was reported use what I'd call harsh or discontinuous metrics, things like exact string match or multiple-choice accuracy. Exact match on, say, a multi-digit arithmetic problem gives you credit only if every single token is right. So imagine the model's per-token accuracy is improving smoothly and predictably with scale, which is roughly what you'd expect from scaling laws on cross-entropy loss. If the answer is ten tokens long, the probability of getting the whole thing exactly right is roughly that per-token accuracy raised to the tenth power. That nonlinear transformation takes a smooth, steady improvement and squashes it down to essentially zero for a long time, and then it shoots up. So the absence of signal for small models isn't that nothing is happening; it's that the metric is throwing away all the partial progress.

And we tested this a few ways. One was simply to take the same model outputs and score them with continuous or more forgiving metrics, like token edit distance or Brier score instead of accuracy. When you do that, the sharp jumps largely go away, and you see smooth, predictable improvement, including meaningful signal in the small models that looked like they were at zero. The second piece is statistical resolution. If you have a small test set, you literally can't distinguish an accuracy of 0.001 from zero, so the curve looks flat purely because you don't have enough samples. If you increase the evaluation data, you start resolving above-chance performance in the smaller models. And third, we showed you can go the other way: take vision models, where nobody was claiming emergence, choose a sharp metric, and you can manufacture what looks like emergent behavior.

Now, I want to be careful about what we're claiming. We're not saying no capability can ever appear abruptly, or that scale doesn't matter. There may well be genuine phase transitions in some settings. And the metrics people care about in practice are often the harsh ones; if you need the exact right answer, then partial credit isn't what a user experiences. So the abruptness can be real from a downstream-utility perspective. The point is more scientific: if what you want is to understand and predict how capabilities develop, you should be suspicious of a flat-then-jump curve, and check whether a smoother metric or more evaluation data reveals continuous progress underneath. That matters a lot for things like forecasting and safety, because the story "abilities appear unpredictably out of nowhere" leads to very different conclusions than "abilities improve predictably and we just weren't measuring finely enough."

r001.rationale: The response says small test sets cannot distinguish accuracy of 0.001 from zero and that more evaluation data reveals above-chance performance in smaller models.

r002.rationale: It describes performance as improving smoothly and predictably with scale, including meaningful underlying progress in small models.

r003.rationale: It explains that more samples are needed to resolve a low correct-answer probability, using 0.001 accuracy as the example.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the crux of the work we did on the "mirage" question. The claim in a lot of the emergence literature is that for some task, performance is essentially flat at zero across a whole range of smaller models, and then at some scale it just takes off. And the natural interpretation people reach for is that something qualitative changed inside the model, some capability switched on.

Our argument is that the apparent absence of a signal in the small models is often a property of how you're measuring, not a property of the model. If your metric is something like exact-match accuracy on a multi-step arithmetic problem, that's a nonlinear, all-or-nothing transformation of what the model is actually doing. A model that gets nine of ten digits right scores the same as a model that gets zero right. So the small models might be improving steadily, token by token, and you've chosen a metric that's blind to that improvement until the model crosses the threshold where every piece is correct at once.

And when you go back and look with a smoother metric, say token-level edit distance or per-token log-likelihood of the correct answer, the "flat then sudden jump" picture usually dissolves into a fairly smooth, predictable curve. The signal was there in the small models all along. We just weren't looking at it in a way that could register it. We also showed you can go the other way and manufacture emergence in settings where nobody would claim there's anything emergent, like vision models, just by picking a discontinuous metric.

So my interpretation of the "absence" is mostly a measurement artifact, compounded by a resolution problem. If your small models are only evaluated on a few hundred examples, and their true accuracy is, say, half a percent, you'll see zero and conclude there's nothing there. More test data, or finer-grained scoring, would show you the gradient.

Now, I want to be careful. We're not claiming nothing interesting ever happens with scale. There may be genuine phase transitions in some settings. What we're saying is that the standard evidence for emergence doesn't distinguish between "a capability appeared" and "a metric finally became sensitive." And that matters a lot practically, because the whole concern about unpredictability, that we can't forecast what a bigger model will do, is really a claim about the smooth metric. If the underlying quantity is predictable, you can forecast it, and then the question of when the discontinuous metric flips becomes an engineering question about thresholds, not a mystery.

r001.rationale: It says limited evaluation on a few hundred examples can make a small model’s signal appear absent, and that more test data would reveal it.

r002.rationale: The response describes steady improvement and a smooth, predictable curve, but does not clearly state that performance increases monotonically with model size in the small-model regime.

r003.rationale: It explains that a true accuracy as low as half a percent may appear as zero on a few hundred examples and that more test data would reveal the signal.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be careful about interpreting the absence of a signal as the absence of a capability. The metric you choose can hide gradual improvements. If you’re measuring exact-match accuracy, for example, a model gets no credit until it produces the entire answer correctly. A smaller model might be getting progressively closer, but that progress doesn’t show up in the score.

Then, as you scale up, you cross that threshold and suddenly see a jump. That can look like a capability appeared out of nowhere, even though the underlying improvement was smooth. So I’d want to look at more sensitive measures before concluding that there was nothing happening in the smaller models. That doesn’t rule out emergence; it means the apparent discontinuity alone isn’t enough to establish it.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the missing signal to metric insensitivity, not insufficient sampling.

r002.rationale: It describes gradual underlying improvement as a possibility, but does not state that performance is expected to increase monotonically with model size in the small-model regime.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss estimating low probabilities or the need for more samples.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about interpreting the absence of a measured signal as the absence of an underlying capability. What you see depends a lot on how you measure performance. If your metric is exact match, for example, a model gets no credit until it produces the entire answer correctly. It could be improving steadily and still look like it’s doing nothing, until suddenly it crosses that threshold.

So the question is whether the capability itself changes abruptly, or whether the measurement makes a gradual change look abrupt. Looking at a more continuous measure—say, the probability assigned to the correct answer—can help distinguish those possibilities. That doesn’t mean every claim of emergence is a measurement artifact, but a flat curve for small models alone isn’t enough to establish that the underlying ability is absent.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the apparent absence of a signal to measurement choice, but does not mention insufficient sampling.

r002.rationale: It discusses a potentially gradual change in performance, but does not state that performance should increase monotonically with model size, including for small models.

r003.rationale: It suggests using the probability assigned to the correct answer, but does not explain that estimating a low probability reliably requires more samples.
